kv.memory.determinable-vs-consumer-shape: When grinding a hardening epic, sort the issues into 'determinable' and 'consumer-shaped' and treat them differently. Determinable = an RFC, a monotonicity property, or plain logic fixes the right answer (OCSP thisUpdate monotonicity, lock-poisoning recovery, clock-per-check instead of a captured timestamp, cache field privacy). Build those. Consumer-shaped = the right answer depends on what a consumer needs to emit or call, and no consumer exists yet (a telemetry observer: which fields -- latency, HTTP status, bytes, cache hit rate? a batch API: concurrency, ordering, partial-failure semantics?). Do NOT invent those blind; you commit public API in a guessed shape and then keep it for compatibility. Instead record the analysis on the bead -- what the channel options are, why the obvious one is blocked, what is already possible with existing public API -- so the design is cheap when a consumer turns up. PKIX-cr8: built 8, deferred 2 on exactly this line.
kv.memory.don-t-duplicate-isn-t-the-rule: Don't duplicate' isn't the rule -- 'don't duplicate code where a divergence would be a security bug' is. Two calls one day apart in the MTA-STS work went opposite ways and both were right: EXTRACTED pkix-aia-http's destination policy into pkix-net-guard (subtle address classification -- NAT64, IPv4-mapped, RFC 6598 -- where a second copy silently wrong is an SSRF hole), but did NOT extract pkix-dane-resolver's UpstreamConfig (parsing a name server address; a second copy can't cause a security bug, and sharing it would mean depending on pkix-dane + pkix-dnssec-anchor to parse a SocketAddr). Test for the distinction: would a divergence between the copies be exploitable, or merely untidy?
kv.memory.mta-sts-and-dane-need-opposite: MTA-STS and DANE need OPPOSITE resolver configurations in the same workspace, and both are correct. pkix-dane-resolver sets hickory validate=true and refuses unvalidated answers (RFC 7672 §2.1.1: indeterminate TLSA == insecure; DANE's trust basis IS DNSSEC). pkix-mta-sts-resolver must NOT require DNSSEC (RFC 8461 §1 relies on CAs and 'does not require DNSSEC, at a cost of risking malicious downgrades'; the _mta-sts TXT record carries no authentication at all -- it's a change token pointing at a policy whose trust comes from the HTTPS cert). Requiring validation there would refuse policies from most conforming domains. Same for profiles: MTA-STS §4.2 requires a SAN so BasicTlsProfile is right, while SMTP DANE per RFC 7672 §3.2.3 consults commonName so BasicSmtpMtaProfile requires neither SAN nor EKU.
kv.memory.rustflags-d-warnings-not-inher: CI parity needs BOTH: RUSTFLAGS=-D warnings AND RUSTDOCFLAGS=-D warnings. RUSTFLAGS does NOT reach rustdoc, so a broken or private intra-doc link is only a warning locally while quality-gates (which sets both workflow-wide) fails on it. That exact gap broke the gate on 2bdf3216: public docs on CachedHttpOcspFetcher linked to the private fn is_staler_ocsp, and a local 'RUSTFLAGS=-D warnings cargo doc --all-features' passed. Clippy also does NOT run in the bare-metal or feature-combination jobs, so an unused import or a dead pub(crate) item is a warning locally and an error there -- and it bites hardest on cfg-gated code, where an item used only by feature-gated code is dead in the no-feature build (pkix-tlsrpt classify imports, pkix-aia-http is_public, time::Clock in pkix-revocation-http). Full local gate: export RUSTFLAGS='-D warnings' RUSTDOCFLAGS='-D warnings'; cargo fmt --all --check; cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features; cargo doc --workspace --all-features --no-deps; cargo hack check --workspace --feature-powerset --depth 2 -- WORKSPACE-wide, never per-crate.
kv.memory.when-a-documented-gap-gets-clo: When a documented gap gets closed, INVERT the test that pinned it rather than deleting it. pkix-tlsrpt had a test asserting NOTHING maps to sts-webpki-invalid (because FetchError::Transport conflated a TLS failure with a network one). After adding FetchError::TlsValidation, the test became 'only TlsValidation maps to it, and Transport explicitly does not' -- the harm guarded against never changed, only the ability to distinguish the cases. A future change folding the variants back together still fails there.
